en: The Ritual Manual for Monks;
Homage to the Omniscient One.

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen. I, named so-and-so, request from the Saṃgha the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk. May the venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me full ordination, having taken pity on me. (This should be said three times.
After it has been requested, one monk should sit down and make the following proclamation:
"Let the venerable Saṃgha listen. This person requests from the Saṃgha the going forth and full ordination, the state of a monk.

If it seems the right time to the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha grant that it shall give the going forth and full ordination to one named so-and-so. This is the motion (*jñapti*). It should be done in this manner."

"Let the venerable Saṃgha listen: this person, named so-and-so, requests from the Saṃgha the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk. Therefore, the Saṃgha grants the going forth and confers the full ordination upon the one named so-and-so. Those venerable ones who consent to granting the going forth and conferring the full ordination upon the one named so-and-so should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak."
"This is the first formal proclamation;

likewise a second and a third time. So-and-so has been ordained and fully admitted by the Saṅgha. It is approved and consented to by the Saṅgha, since there is silence; thus do I understand this to be so."
[This is indeed the preliminary rite:
Pay heed! I, named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion.
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies. May the Venerable One accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) for as long as life lasts.

Pay heed, O Teacher: just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life, so too I, [name], for as long as life lasts, abstain from the taking of life.
By this first limb, I train in, conform to, and emulate the training of those noble Arhats.

Just as those noble ones, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, have abstained from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants— even so do I, [named so-and-so], for as long as life lasts, abandon taking what is not given...

Having abandoned sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, I abstain from the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.

By this fifth limb, I train after them, I conform to them, and I imitate the training of those noble Arhats. Venerable sirs, may you attend to me: I, named so-and-so, having taken white garments from my preceptor named so-and-so, with hair and beard not yet shorn, desire the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

"I, who am so-and-so, with such-and-such a name as my preceptor, shall go forth from the home to the homeless state out of right faith in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, having shaved off hair and beard and donned saffron robes.
Let him go forth!
Pay heed, Preceptor; I, so-and-so, request the Preceptor as my Upādhyāya."
"May the teacher be my preceptor;
through the teacher as preceptor, I shall go forth.
Pay heed, Preceptor: I, who am named so-and-so, from this day forward for as long as life lasts, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds."
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of all things free from passion;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of all assemblies.
I follow in the renunciation of that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Sovereign King of the Śākyas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"I renounce the marks of the householder; I adopt the marks of the wandering life. Thus a second and a third time.
Pay heed, Venerable Sir! I, who am named so-and-so, from this day forward for as long as life lasts, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of two-legged beings;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of things free from passion;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies.
"May the Venerable One accept me as a *śrāmaṇera* for as long as life lasts.

[Thus a second and a third time. "Pay attention, Preceptor: just as those noble Arhats, having abandoned taking life for as long as life lasts, abstained from taking life, even so I, named so-and-so, for as long as life lasts, [abstain from taking life]."
Having abandoned the taking of life, I abstain from it.
By this first limb, I train in accordance with, conform to, and emulate the training of those noble Arhats.

Just as those noble Arhats have for their entire lives abstained from taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, so do I likewise.

Having abandoned dancing, singing, instrumental music, wearing garlands, using perfumes and ointments, and applying cosmetics; having abandoned high and luxurious beds, and the acceptance of gold and silver; being abstinent from the acceptance of gold and silver—even so, I, [name], for as long as life lasts, shall abstain from taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, the state of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, and dancing, singing, instrumental music, wearing garlands, using perfumes and ointments, and applying cosmetics.
Having abandoned high beds, luxurious beds, eating at improper times, and the acceptance of gold and silver, I abstain from the acceptance of gold and silver.
By this tenth limb, I train in accordance with, conform to, and emulate the training of those noble Arhats.
Pay heed, Venerable Sir; I, [name], request the Venerable Upādhyāya.
"May the Venerable One be my preceptor;
with the Venerable One as preceptor, I shall receive full ordination.
Pay heed, Preceptor: I, named so-and-so, consecrate this robe, the outer cloak (saṃghāṭī), as a determined robe for use."

Pay attention, Preceptor: I, [name], designate this robe as an upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*); it is a determined robe, fit for use. Pay attention, Preceptor: I, [name], designate this robe as an inner robe (*antarvāsa*); it is a determined robe, fit for use. Pay attention, Preceptor: I designate this robe as an outer cloak (*saṃghāṭī*).
Desiring to make it new, I shall run,
spread out, cut, join together, stitch, sew, and dye the two and a half maṇḍalakas without hindrance; or I shall apply patches here to the robe for use.
Pay attention, Preceptor: I, [name], this very person, consecrate this robe as an upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Desiring it, I shall make seven [patches];
I shall wash, stretch, cut, join, knot, and sew it into two and a half circular patches without any obstacle.
I shall preserve it. I will place this used robe upon my attendants here.
Pay heed, Preceptor: I, [name], designate this robe as an inner garment (*antarvāsa*).
Desiring [to finish], I shall make the fivefold [process]:
I shall wash, stretch, cut, join, knot, sew, dye, and preserve it;
or I shall attach patches here to make it a robe fit for use.
"Pay attention, Preceptor! I, who am named so-and-so, have this bowl, a vessel for sages, a vessel for alms, for personal use.
I, named so-and-so, have requested [the monk] named so-and-so as my private instructor. You, named so-and-so, are you able to instruct me, named so-and-so, in private?

[He replies: 'I am able, with the preceptor named so-and-so. Let the venerable Saṃgha listen: this monk, named so-and-so, is able to instruct the one named so-and-so in private, with the preceptor named so-and-so."
If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant its permission: this monk named so-and-so shall instruct in private the monk named so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor. This is the motion.
Listen, venerable one: this is the time for you to speak the truth.
This is the time for truth.
Whatever I ask you, you must not be ashamed; you should speak what is real as real, and what is unreal as unreal, and not conceal it. Are you a man?
Are you a male endowed with the male faculty?
"You are twenty years of age;
you possess a complete set of three robes and a bowl;
and your mother and father are living."
Have you been permitted by your mother and father? Are you not a slave? Are you not one who has been brought by force?
Not one who has arrived [prematurely];
not one who is subject to censure; not one who is sold.
May you not be a royal soldier;
may you not be a royal offender; may you not be one who carries out the king's secret tasks.
May you not be a king who has performed or caused to be performed a path-destroying deed; may you not be a thief who hangs from a banner;
may you not be a hemp-weaver.
May you not be a eunuch;
may you not be one who has violated a nun; may you not be one who lives in association with thieves.
May you not be one who dwells apart from the community;
may you not be a matricide;
may you not be a patricide.
May you not be a murderer of an Arhat; may you not be a schismatic of the Saṃgha;
may you not be one who, with a malicious mind, sheds the blood of a Tathāgata.
Do not be a Naga; do not be a beast.
You must not owe anything to anyone, whether little or much; nor are you able to grant full ordination.
Did you go forth previously?
Have you fallen into any one of the four *pārājika* offenses? Are you one who has gone forth now, and have you correctly practiced the holy life?
"What is your name? What is the name of your preceptor?
Listen, venerable one."
Indeed, such bodily ailments as these occur in the bodies of men; namely,
leprosy, boils, and so forth.
Kiṭibha, kilāsa, dadru, and kaṇḍu.
Scabies, silver, cholera.
Eczema, hiccups, and fever.
Consumption, cough, asthma, and wasting.
Epilepsy, the copper-marked [disease], and consumption.
Anemia,
pain in the limbs,
and abdominal tumors with blood.
Fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and vomiting.
Urinary disease, elephantiasis, exhaustion, and burning sensation in the limbs.
Burning pain in the sides; breaking pain in the bones;
the quotidian fever.
The second-day [fever],
the third-day [fever],
the fourth-day [fever].
Constant fever, intermittent fever, and the derangement of the three humors.
May no such bodily afflictions, or others of a similar nature, be found in your body,
now that you have been questioned by me.
The wise fellow-celibates will question you right here in the midst of the Saṃgha.
In that regard, you must not be ashamed; you should speak of what is real as being real, and confess what is unreal as being unreal.
Stay!
Do not come unless you have been summoned.
Let the venerable Saṃgha listen: I, named so-and-so, have been thus instructed by my preceptor, named so-and-so, regarding the obstructive factors in private.
What should come?

Let the venerable Saṃgha listen: I, named so-and-so—mentioning my name for the sake of the matter—seeking full ordination with the preceptor named so-and-so, request full ordination from the Saṃgha; may the venerable Saṃgha ordain me with the preceptor named so-and-so.
May the venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, grant me its favor by following my request.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen: this person named so-and-so, seeking full ordination from the one named so-and-so, requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with so-and-so as preceptor.

If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and if the Saṅgha deems it appropriate, may the Saṅgha permit us to question this person named so-and-so regarding the obstructing factors within the midst of the Saṅgha, with so-and-so as preceptor.
This is the motion.
Listen, venerable one; all this for you is as before. Let the venerable Saṃgha listen: this person, named so-and-so, seeking full ordination from the one named so-and-so, is twenty years of age.
His three robes and alms bowl are complete;
he declares himself pure regarding the obstructing factors.
This person, of such-and-such a name, requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with such-and-such a name as preceptor.
If it seems the right time to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha permit and authorize that the Saṃgha ordain the one named so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Let the venerable Saṃgha listen: this person named so-and-so, seeking ordination from the one named so-and-so, is twenty years of age.
His three robes and alms bowl are complete;
he declares himself pure regarding the obstructing factors.

Such-and-so-named, with such-and-so-named as preceptor, requests full ordination from the Saṅgha. Therefore, the Saṅgha grants full ordination to such-and-so-named, with such-and-so-named as preceptor.
Those venerable ones who approve of ordaining the one named so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor should remain silent;
those who do not approve should speak.
This is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*).
Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
The Saṃgha has ordained [the one named] so-and-so with [the preceptor named] so-and-so; it is approved and permitted because of the silence. Thus do I understand this.
Listen, venerable one: these four [offenses] have been taught by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees.

The Fully Awakened One has thus declared these supports for a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination; relying upon which, a monk’s state of having gone forth, received full ordination, and being a monk occurs within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Are you, [Name], able to subsist for as long as life lasts on robes made of dust-heap rags?
I am able [to accept] an extra gain: a cloth, or an upper garment, or silk, or *āmila* wool, or *kṛmivarṇa* wool, or *samavarṇa* wool, or *durvarṇa* wool,
or wool, or fine wool, or hemp, or linen, or cotton, or *dukūla* cloth, or *kautmapaka* cloth.
Whether it be for this life or for the next world, or whatever other suitable robe-cloth may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual— in that regard, you must exercise moderation in acceptance.
You might encounter such a situation.

"I shall attain full awakening. Listen, [you] of such-and-such a name: by relying upon alms-food as a permissible and easily obtained meal, there is for a monk the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Are you, [you] of such-and-such a name, able to subsist for as long as life lasts on alms-food as your nourishment?"

I am able; there are extra gains, such as meals, or refreshments, or rice gruel, or drinks, or [food] on the fifth day, or on the eighth day, or on the fourteenth day, or on the fifteenth day, or daily food, or by invitation, or on special occasions.
"Or a lump," meaning that whatever other permissible alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) may arise, whether from the Saṅgha or from an individual, you must exercise moderation in accepting it.
"I shall fully awaken to such a state."

I shall attain perfect awakening. Listen, [you] of such-and-such a name: the root of a tree is suitable and easily obtained among lodgings and seats; by relying upon it, for a monk, there is the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣu within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Are you, [you] of such-and-such a name, able to sustain yourself for as long as life lasts by means of a lodging at the root of a tree?
I am able [to provide] extra acquisitions: dwellings, or huts, or gabled houses, or upper chambers, or attic rooms, or buildings with roofs shaped like *āmalaka* fruits,
or those with thatched roofs, or those with plank roofs, or mountain caves, or caves in ravines, or grass huts.

Whether it be a leaf-hut, a place where a walking-path has been made, or one where no walking-path has been made, or whatever other suitable lodging for reclining or sitting may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual— in that case as well, you must exercise moderation in accepting it.
Will you be able to endure such a place?
"I shall attain full enlightenment.

Listen, [Name]: that which is suitable and easily obtained among medicines made from fermented urine—relying upon which, for a monk in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, there is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk—are you, [Name], able to subsist for as long as life lasts on fermented urine as medicine?"

I am able [to accept]: as extra acquisitions, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, that which is kept for a day, that which is kept for a watch of the night, that which is kept for seven days, that which is kept for life;
and medicinal roots, medicinal stalks, medicinal leaves, medicinal flowers, and medicinal fruits.
Furthermore, whatever other suitable medicine may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual, you must exercise moderation in accepting it as well.
Will you be able to fully comprehend such a situation?
I shall attain full enlightenment.

Listen, [you] of such-and-such a name: these four dharma-s of downfall have been declared by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for a monk who has thus gone forth and received ordination; having committed even one of them...
By the mere commission of such an offense, a monk ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, and ceases to be a son of the Śākyas; he falls from the state of a monk.

His śramaṇahood is destroyed, ruined, shattered, fallen, and defeated; his śramaṇahood cannot be restored. It is just as a palm tree whose crown is cut off: it is incapable of becoming green again, incapable of growth, development, or reaching fruition.

Which four? In many ways, sensual pleasures have been censured; sensual pleasures have been described as being the very nature of desire and as being bound by desire. For those who have mastered their desires, the abandonment [of desire] has been praised: its relinquishment, its coming to an end, its destruction, its fading away, its cessation, its pacification, and it has been extolled on all sides.
It has been described and praised:
"From this day forward, O Venerable One, you must not look upon a woman with a lustful mind even by casting a glance;
how much less so should you engage in unchaste sexual intercourse through the union of two persons?"
And this has been said, O Venerable One, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees: "If a monk,

having entered into the commonality of training with the other monks, should engage in unchaste sexual intercourse— even with an animal— without having renounced the training and without having disclosed his weakness in the training, having committed such an offense..."
Through a communal transgression, one ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, and ceases to be a son of the Śākyas; he is destroyed from the state of a monk.
His śramaṇahood is slain, ruined, crushed, fallen, defeated, and his śramaṇahood becomes irrecoverable.
It is just like a palmyra tree whose crown has been cut off: it is incapable of further growth, increase, or expansion.
From this day forward, you must apply yourself with intense resolve and protective mindfulness to refrain from blameworthy conduct and transgressions;
you must not commit any such act.
[He replies: "I shall not commit it."

Listen, venerable one! In many ways the Blessed One has prohibited and censured taking what is not given; he has praised, extolled, lauded, and commended the abstention from taking what is not given. From this day forward, venerable one, you must not, with a thieving mind, take even a husk of sesame belonging to another that has not been given, much less five māṣas or more than five māṣas. This, venerable one, has been said by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—who knows and sees.

Furthermore, if a monk should take from others what has not been given—whether in a village or in the wilderness—considered to be theft, such that for taking what was not given, a king or a royal minister might seize him and either execute him, imprison him, or banish him, saying to him:
"O man, you are a thief! You are a fool! You are a deluded one! You are a robber!"—if he should commit such an act;
Through a communal transgression, he ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, ceases to be a son of the Śākyas; he is destroyed from the state of a monk.
His śramaṇahood is ruined, crushed, fallen, defeated, and becomes irrecoverable.
It is just like a palmyra tree whose head has been cut off—it is incapable of becoming green again, incapable of sprouting, growing, or reaching maturity.
In this regard, you must apply yourself with a keen mind, protective mindfulness, and vigilance to the abstention from the blameworthy conduct and transgressions that you have previously committed.
You shall not commit any such offense;
[I shall not commit it].
Listen, O [Name], in many ways the Blessed One has censured the taking of life; he has praised, extolled, honored, and commended the abstention from taking life.
From this day forward, O Venerable One, you must not intentionally deprive any living being of life, even an ant, let alone a human body.
And this, O Venerable One, was said by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees.

Furthermore, if a monk should intentionally deprive a human being or one who has the form of a human being of life with his own hand; or if he should provide them with a weapon; or seek out a wielder of a weapon for them; or incite them to death; or describe the praises of death to them.

And he should speak to him thus: "O man, what is the use of this wretched, impure, and miserable life for you? O man, death is better than life! With such thoughts and mental intentions, he would, in many ways, incite him toward death or describe the praises of death to him; and if he were to die because of that, it is of such a nature [that constitutes a pārājika offense].
A monk, having committed such an offense, by that very commission ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, and ceases to be a son of the Śākyas.
He is fallen from the state of a monk; his status as a śramaṇa is destroyed, ruined, shattered, fallen, defeated, and his śramaṇahood becomes irrecoverable.
Just as a palmyra tree with its crown cut off is incapable of becoming green again, and incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion.
"From this day forward, you must apply yourself with a keen mind, constant mindfulness, and vigilance to the avoidance of blameworthy conduct and transgressions. You shall not fall into such a state;
I myself shall not fall into it.
Listen, Venerable One! In many ways, the Blessed One has censured false speech, and he has praised, extolled, honored, and commended the abstention from false speech."

"From this day forward, Venerable One, you must not speak even a deliberate lie, even for the sake of a joke; how much less so should you prattle about a non-existent, unattained superhuman state (uttara-manuṣya-dharma)?
And this has been said, Venerable One, by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Awakened One—who knows and sees:
'Whosoever is a monk who, without direct knowledge and without full realization, [claims] a non-existent, unattained superhuman state, a noble distinction of attainment...'"

If one should claim knowledge, or vision, or a state of pleasant abiding, saying, "I know this; I see this," and being questioned or not questioned at a later time, he—having fallen into an offense and seeking purification—should say: "Venerable sir, not knowing, I said 'I know'; not seeing, I said 'I see. This was empty, vain, and a false pretense, except for mere overestimation (*abhimāna*)."
This monk also is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Do you understand?
I understand suffering.
I know the origin, the cessation, and the path.
What do you see?
I see the gods.
“I see nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas;
the gods also see me;
the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas also see me.”
I hear the voice of the gods;
I hear the voices of the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas;
and the gods also hear my voice.
Even the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas, hear my voice;
I approach to see the gods,
and I approach to see the nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas.
Even the gods approach me for the sake of seeing me; even the nāgas, and so on, up to the kaṭapūtanas, approach me for the sake of seeing me.
I converse with the gods, I chat with them, I greet them, and I maintain constant association with them.
I converse with the nāgas, and so on, up to the kaṭapūtanas, I chat with them, I greet them, and I maintain constant association with them.
Even the gods converse with me, talk with me, greet me, and engage in constant association.
Even the nāgas, up to the kaṭapūtanas, also converse with me, talk with me, greet me, and engage in constant association.
Dwelling in what is unattainable, through the perception of impermanence, he declares of himself: "I am one who has attained."

By means of the perception of suffering in the impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of lack of delight in the entire world, the perception of light, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, and the perception of death;
while dwelling in a secluded place, by means of the perception of the foul and not the perception of the beautiful, he recognizes himself, saying, "I am one who has no desire."

By means of the perception of the livid corpse, the perception of the festering corpse, the perception of the dismembered corpse, the perception of the worm-infested corpse, the perception of the gnawed corpse, the perception of the blood-stained corpse, the perception of the scattered corpse, the perception of the skeleton, and the perception of the contemplation of emptiness, he declares: "I am one who has attained mastery. Dwelling in solitude, he attains mastery over the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as over loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Of compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, [the fruit of arhatship],
the domain of supernormal powers, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, and the recollection of past lives.

Even though he is not yet an Arhat, one who claims of himself, "I am a meditator on the eight liberations," except as a mere pretense—by falling into such a state, a monk becomes fallen through that very transgression; he is no longer a monk, no longer a son of the Śākyas. He is ruined from his status as a monk; his asceticism is destroyed, shattered, crushed, fallen, and defeated, and it cannot be restored for him.
Just as a palmyra tree whose head has been cut off is incapable of becoming green again, and incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion, so too,

from this day forward, regarding this transgression, I must apply myself with an intense mind, guarded mindfulness, and vigilance to the avoidance of such misconduct, so that I do not commit even the slightest offense.
Should I fall into even a single such state, [it would be as described].
I shall not transgress.
Indeed, these dharmas leading to downfall have been declared;
therefore, the dharmas that constitute the state of a śramaṇa must now be declared.

Listen, venerable one: these four qualities that make one a true ascetic were proclaimed by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees. What are the four?
From this day forward, venerable one, when you are reviled, you must not revile in return; when you are provoked to anger, you must not be provoked in return.
When struck, one should not strike back; when reviled, one should not revile in return.
"Will you commit any such offense?
"I will not commit it.
"Listen, Āyuṣmat! You who previously had this aspiration: 'May I obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.'"
This person has now gone forth and received full ordination with a suitable preceptor and two suitable teachers,

by a complete Saṃgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation— which is irreversible and not subject to suspension— such that what must be trained in by a monk who has been ordained for a hundred years must be trained in by one who has been ordained on that very day; therein lies the equality of conduct and the equality of training.

The recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra in common must henceforth be fulfilled and not neglected. From this day forward, you should maintain the perception of your preceptor as a father, and your preceptor should likewise maintain the perception of you as a son. From this day forward, your preceptor is to be served by you for as long as life lasts.
The preceptor must also attend to you when you are ill, until you recover or until death occurs.
From this day forward, you must dwell with reverence, respect, and a sense of awe toward your fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether they be seniors, those of middle standing, or juniors.
From this day forward, you must teach, recite, and study, and you must become skilled in the aggregates (*skandha*) and skilled in the elements (*dhātu*).

Skill in the sense bases must be practiced, skill in dependent origination, skill in what is possible and impossible, and you must lay down the burden for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, for the sake of realizing what has not been realized, and for the sake of manifesting what has not been manifested. Furthermore, these most fundamental rules of training have been declared by me to you, or others [to be recited] every half-month.
"When the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra is being performed, you will hear it; furthermore, your preceptor and teacher will cause you to master other [teachings].

Your fellow-students, those with the same preceptor, those with the same teacher, your trusted friends, those who converse with you, those who live together with you, and those who are affectionate toward you—all these are yours.
Thus have you been fully ordained within the teaching of the One of Excellent Wisdom."
So that you do not lose this rare attainment of the opportune moment—
this pleasing full ordination of one purified by going forth—
has indeed been proclaimed by the Fully Awakened One, who knows all and whose name is Truth.
You have now received full ordination; apply yourself with diligence.
The ritual formula is completed.
